title: AMAT with Two Levels of Cache
unit: Memory Interfacing, Hierarchy and Cache Mapping
quickIdea: Each level's miss penalty is the next level's own access time plus its miss rate times its penalty: AMAT = T1 + m1 x (T2 + m2 x T3), and the multiplication is what makes a slow last level cheap.
remember: Write the recursion once and it answers every multi-level question: AMAT = T1 + m1 x (T2 + m2 x (T3 + ...)).
m1 is the L1 miss rate, m2 the L2 miss rate counted among L1 misses - not among all accesses.
The fraction of accesses that reach main memory is m1 x m2, so a level deep in the hierarchy contributes only through the product of the miss rates above it.

When a question gives a miss penalty in nanoseconds instead of an access time, that penalty is already the extra time on top of the level above, so it goes in the bracket without adding the upper level's time again.
An inclusive hierarchy writes back into the upper level, so a miss in L2 also costs the transfer to L1; an exclusive one does not.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.45: L1 access 1 ns with a 90% hit rate; L2 hit rate 80% with a 10 ns miss penalty from L2 to L1; 100 ns miss penalty from memory to L2. Find the AMAT.

gateAngle: GATE has asked this twice recently, once with access times and once with penalties, and the difference between the two forms is exactly the trap. The other trap is applying m2 to all accesses instead of to L1 misses.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.45, as worked above.
variations.why: 0.2 x 100 is the memory term inside the bracket; the bracket is the L1 miss penalty, and 0.1 of it is added to the 1 ns hit time.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Same system, but the question instead states the L2 access time as 11 ns (not a 10 ns penalty) and the memory access time as 100 ns. What changes?
variations.answer: Nothing numerically: 1 + 0.1 x (11 + 0.2 x 100) = 1 + 0.1 x 31 = 4.1 ns. The bracket is now built from access times, so the L2 term is 11 rather than 1 + 10.
variations.why: It is the same arithmetic with the hit time folded in. Reading whether a number is an access time or a penalty is the whole skill.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does making L2 larger and slower sometimes leave AMAT unchanged?
variations.answer: Because its contribution is m1 x m2 x T3-weighted: if m1 is 0.05, an extra 10 ns at L2 adds only 0.5 ns.
variations.why: It explains why real designs put a large slow L3 below a small fast L2 rather than making L2 large.

trap.what: Applying the L2 miss rate to every access rather than to L1 misses.
trap.why: L2 is only consulted when L1 misses, so the memory term must be multiplied by m1 as well as m2.
trap.counterexample: In the 2025 question, charging memory to all accesses gives 1 + 0.1 x 10 + 0.2 x 100 = 22 ns instead of 4 ns - a five-fold error from one missing multiplication.

check.question: L1: 1 ns, 95% hit. L2: 8 ns, 90% hit. Memory: 80 ns. What is the AMAT?
check.explanation: Only 0.5% of accesses reach memory (0.05 x 0.1), so the 80 ns level contributes 0.4 ns on average.
